name: Han dynasty imperial army (c. 200 BC - AD 100)

weightNotes.aggression: Under Emperor Wu the Han took the war to the steppe: Longcheng raid 129 BC, Hexi and Ordos campaigns, Mobei 119 BC, Dayuan 104-102 BC, Zhizhi 36 BC, Dou Xian's 50,000 cavalry in AD 89 (Han-Xiongnu War pages). Lowered because the first seventy years after Baideng (200 BC) were heqin appeasement.
weightNotes.maneuver: Long-distance cavalry expeditions in multiple columns (Mobei: two columns of 50,000 cavalry), but the infantry core fought positionally from wagon laagers (Mobei page). Middling-high.
weightNotes.flanking: At Mobei the Han shock cavalry 'encircled the Chanyu's army from both flanks' under cover of a sandstorm, and Lu Bode's division took a flanking route; Li Guang's flanking column got lost and missed the battle (Mobei page).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Capable of sieges (Dayuan 102 BC: engineers diverted the river and cut the city's water; Zhizhi 36 BC: citadel stormed and burned), but the strategic target was the nomad field army (War of the Heavenly Horses, Zhizhi pages).
weightNotes.reserveUse: Wei Qing held 5,000 cavalry inside the wagon ring to deal with breakthroughs before committing it to the envelopment (Mobei page). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Frontier beacon and watch-post system with careful records (Military of the Han page), but in the field intelligence failed often: a prisoner's misinformation reshuffled the Mobei columns, Li Guang got lost, Gaozu was lured into encirclement at Baideng (200 BC).
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.iron mid 0.14, grade C. Previous 0.5 came from Li Ling 99 BC, 92% lost, a total that includes a days-long fighting retreat and the surrender (Li Ling page); the retreat began before the heavy losses, so it is no evidence of holding. Han law executing failed generals (Military of the Han page) pushes the other way. No source supports a profile-specific value: era baseline.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Crossbow infantry, armoured war wagons (wugang chariots), cavalry and archers in one formation; at Mobei the wagon ring sheltered archers, crossbowmen and infantry while cavalry manoeuvred (Mobei page). The crossbow gave Han forces a 'slight advantage' (Military of the Han page).
weightNotes.initiative: Column commanders operated weeks apart in the steppe, but under heavy penalties for failure and with the emperor redirecting columns (Mobei); Li Guang's suicide shows the system punished, not rewarded, independent judgment.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Expeditions needed huge trains (second Dayuan expedition: 60,000 men with 100,000 oxen and 20,000 donkeys and camels; it still returned with only 10,000 men), the first Dayuan army starved, and frontier military colonies grew grain for garrisons (War of the Heavenly Horses, Military of the Han pages). Planned but often exceeded.

summary: A large state army, initially conscript and later mostly professional, with a standing force of 600,000-700,000 including about 300,000 cavalry by the late 2nd century BC (Military of the Han page). The infantry fought in deep formations with crossbows and halberds, often behind laagers of armoured war wagons; the cavalry, built up to fight the Xiongnu, made long expeditions into the steppe in converging columns. The frontier was held by walls, beacons and military colonies, and campaigns were organised by a literate bureaucracy that tracked rations and equipment.
whyItWorked: Organisation and resources: the Han could raise, equip and supply forces far larger than any nomad confederation and combine crossbow firepower from a wagon fortress with massed cavalry. Mobei (119 BC) broke the Chanyu's main army, the Hexi corridor and Western Regions were secured, and Zhizhi (36 BC) killed a Xiongnu chanyu far beyond the frontier.
whereItFailed: Distance and supply: the first Dayuan expedition (104 BC) starved, and even the successful second one came back with 10,000 of 60,000 men. Infantry caught in the steppe without support was destroyed (Li Ling, 99 BC). Intelligence failures and the emperor's interference split commands (Baideng 200 BC, the Mobei column switch), and horse losses on each expedition were ruinous.
